text_summary.body: Chapter 12: the nations besiege Jerusalem, which becomes a cup of reeling and a heavy stone; the LORD pours out a spirit of grace and they look on the one they pierced, mourning like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddo. Chapter 13: a fountain is opened for sin, idols and false prophets are removed, and the sword is called against the LORD's shepherd so that the sheep scatter and a third are refined. Chapter 14: the nations take Jerusalem, the LORD fights, his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits, and the people flee as from the earthquake in Uzziah's days; living waters flow, the LORD is king over all the earth, and the nations go up yearly to keep the Feast of Booths.

setting.period: Disputed: after 518 BC (traditional) or late third century BC (Mitchell)
setting.body: Keil assigns chs. 12–14 to Zechariah. Mitchell assigns 12:1–13:6 and ch. 14 to a fourth, apocalyptic writer soon after the battle of Raphia (217 BC), and 13:7–9 to the author of 11:4–17.

rulers.role: King of Persia (on the traditional dating)

constraints.subject: evt_01M4W2B2VAZJFHAYRQ4AK6ZWEM
constraints.textual_assertion: The burden of the word of the LORD concerning Israel
assumptions: Placed after the first burden in book order; Keil treats both as Zechariah's last oracles, Mitchell as later Greek-period additions (see the disputed claim).

terminology.term: Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddo (12:11)
terminology.gloss: The mourning for Josiah, killed at Megiddo (2 Chr 35:22–25); so the Targum, Jerome, Keil and Mitchell; Jerome locates the place near Megiddo (Maximianopolis), identified with Rummaneh. The Adonis/Tammuz view (Hitzig) is rejected by both.

terminology.term: the earthquake in the days of Uzziah (14:5)
terminology.gloss: The earthquake of Amos 1:1; Josephus links it with Uzziah's intrusion into the temple.

competing_reconstructions.label: Zechariah son of Iddo, after 518 BC
A Greek-period apocalyptic writer (c. 217–204 BC)
competing_reconstructions.summary: Later than 9:1–11:3 and written about the same time as 11:4–17, between Raphia and the death of Ptolemy IV.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik reads "me whom they pierced" as Jesus and the mourning as Israel's future national repentance.
Guzik argues that the siege of AD 70 does not fit, because no deliverance followed.
